video_title: Lawfare Daily: Iran War Update—and How We Got Here
gist: Former CIA/DoD officials Ari Tabatabai and Julia Curley argue the roughly seven-month US-Iran war has settled into a grinding negotiate-while-striking phase in which Iran holds the leverage: the conflict has spread from the Strait of Hormuz to the Bab el-Mandeb/Red Sea, Houthis have hit Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline and Riyadh, US munitions and readiness are depleting, and the likeliest endgame is a deal on Iran's terms that includes tolls or tacit control over Hormuz. They attribute the failure to the administration gutting the NSC, interagency process and national-security workforce, and expect no resolution before the US midterms, with a possible congressional power-of-the-purse showdown in the new year.

insights.claim: The Iran war has spread to a second energy chokepoint: Houthi advances down the Red Sea coast are now squeezing the Bab el-Mandeb, on top of the ongoing Strait of Hormuz disruption.
insights.speaker: Ari Tabatabai
insights.so_what: Both main Gulf export routes for oil and gas (including flows to Europe) are now at risk at once, raising the floor under energy prices, tanker rates and shipping insurance.
insights.quote: we now have a second choke point in the region that has been affected by the conflict that is the Babel Mandab and the Red Sea

insights.claim: The Houthis have attacked Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, the route that lets Saudi crude bypass both Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb, and have also struck Riyadh itself.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: The main bypass for Gulf supply is itself under attack, so there are fewer ways around a Hormuz closure. That is bullish for the oil risk premium and bearish for Saudi output reliability.
insights.quote: We had an attack on the East West pipeline that allows Saudi Arabia to export its oil, avoiding both of those two choke points.

insights.claim: Iran's stated terms for a ceasefire include the US lifting its naval blockade, releasing frozen assets, ending the war on all fronts including Lebanon, and Iran keeping at least tacit control over the Strait of Hormuz, likely including the right to charge a percentage toll on shipping.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: A permanent Hormuz toll would add a lasting cost to Gulf energy exports, even in the 'peace' scenario.
insights.quote: probably to charge uh some percentage, which will just then get priced into, you know, global energy exports

insights.claim: Gulf allies are expected to push Washington to either intervene militarily or accept whatever concessions end the war, which likely means letting Iran charge a toll on vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: The political path to ending the war runs through Iran gaining a Hormuz toll, a structural change in how Gulf shipping is priced.
insights.quote: allow them to charge a toll almost certainly uh on vessels coming through the straight

insights.claim: According to BBC reporting cited on the show, an unnamed Iranian official said Iran could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within a week if the US dropped its naval blockade and met other conditions, and that Iran had softened its demands from earlier rounds.
insights.speaker: Natalie Orpet (host)
insights.so_what: A quick reopening is a real tail scenario that would crush the oil risk premium, so watch for any move on the US naval blockade.
insights.quote: indicated that Iran was perhaps prepared to open the straight of Hormuz within a week if the US would drop its naval blockade

insights.claim: US gasoline prices are around $5 a gallon and could reach about $6 a gallon by year-end as a consequence of the Iran war.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: Consumers face an energy shock that drags on discretionary spending and inflation into the midterms and year-end.
insights.quote: the global economic consequences of $5, now probably $6 a gallon gas by the end of the year

themes.theme: Gulf allies exposed, Saudi economic damage

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia has suffered a massive drop in GDP over the last year because of the Iran war and Houthi escalation.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: Saudi and Gulf sovereign credit, equities and fiscal plans are under stress, and the pressure on Riyadh to back any deal is growing.
insights.quote: The Saudis have had a ma massive drop in their GDP over the last year

insights.claim: US military presence in the Gulf has flipped from deterring Iran to making US partners targets, as Houthi escalation against Saudi Arabia and attacks on regional bases continue.
insights.speaker: Ari Tabatabai
insights.so_what: Gulf states may rethink hosting US forces and security alignments, a long-term shift in how risky the region is to invest in.
insights.quote: shift from this notion that US presence in the region served as a deterrent against Iranian aggression to now actually putting a target on the back of uh US partners in the region

insights.claim: According to press reports, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has pressed President Trump for US air support against the Houthis, and Trump has shown strong reluctance to commit more forces ahead of the midterms.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: A US escalation to defend Saudi infrastructure is unlikely before November, so Saudi energy assets stay exposed.

insights.claim: The Houthis act largely independently of Iran. They get material, intelligence and training support from Iran and Hezbollah, but they need no day-to-day approval to escalate against US partners, which makes them a resilient source of horizontal escalation.
insights.speaker: Ari Tabatabai
insights.so_what: A US-Iran deal may not immediately stop Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping, so Red Sea risk could outlast a ceasefire.

insights.claim: Iran's playbook is horizontal escalation through allies and proxies. The Houthis need no instruction to seize openings that strain US allies, because their mission is simply to inflict cost while Iran is under threat.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: Expect escalation to spread geographically, not just intensify, so price risk across all regional shipping lanes and Gulf infrastructure.
insights.quote: It's to cause damage and and pain and complication to US allies and partners while their own ally is under threat.

insights.claim: At the UN General Assembly, Trump predicted a deal with Iran after the US midterm elections, which the analysts read as a tacit admission that the war will not be resolved before November.
insights.speaker: Ari Tabatabai
insights.so_what: Don't expect a pre-November de-escalation to relieve energy prices; the earliest resolution window is after the midterms.
insights.quote: it's almost a tacit acknowledgement by the president that this is not going to get resolved before the midterms

insights.claim: The panel argues Iran, not the US, will decide when the war ends. Iran benefits from waiting for Trump to be further weakened in the midterms, or from locking in a deal while its leverage is at its peak.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: Iran controls the timing of any settlement, so headline-driven rallies on 'progress in talks' are likely to fade.
insights.quote: this war is going to end at a time and place of the Iranians choosing

insights.claim: US-Iran talks (in Pakistan and now in New York) keep producing positive readouts without changing anything on the ground, and Trump's threats to annihilate Iran have lost credibility with regional actors.
insights.speaker: Ari Tabatabai
insights.so_what: Discount both diplomatic optimism and escalation rhetoric as market signals, and watch physical indicators like the blockade and chokepoint status.
insights.quote: we should just hold our horses because we've seen this movie before a few times

insights.claim: US secondary sanctions on Iran's trading partners leave out its main economic lifeline, China. China has been less hurt by the oil price surge because it prepared for this contingency and has no intention of joining a US squeeze on Iran.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: Sanctions won't close the war, and China's energy stockpiling gives it a relative advantage over other importers during the disruption.
insights.quote: who have not been as affected by the global oil price rises because they they've prepared for this contingency

insights.claim: Rolling out large new sanctions on Iran more than six months into active military conflict signals that the administration knows military pressure is not achieving its aims.
insights.speaker: Ari Tabatabai
insights.so_what: Treat late-stage sanctions as a sign of weakness rather than escalation, which supports the view of a drawn-out war.

insights.claim: If the war runs into 2027 and Democrats take Congress, a new Congress could use the power of the purse and oversight hearings to constrain the war, setting up an unprecedented executive-legislative showdown.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: Defense appropriations and war funding become a policy risk in early 2027, which matters for defense contractors and for how long the war lasts.
insights.quote: we could have a real showdown over this war, assuming it continues into the the new year, which it could very well

insights.claim: Congress has given up oversight of the Iran war, letting War Powers Act deadlines pass while the administration claims every 90 days or so that the war has ended and restarted.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: There is no near-term legislative check on the war before the new Congress is seated.

insights.claim: A DoD Inspector General report confirmed that the Iran war is significantly depleting US military capabilities and munitions stocks, and new reporting suggests DoD may be publicly undercounting US service member casualties (at least 19 acknowledged).
insights.speaker: Ari Tabatabai
insights.so_what: Munitions stocks will need replenishing, which supports multi-year demand for missiles and interceptors and defense production.

insights.claim: US readiness costs grow the longer the war lasts. Carriers such as the USS Abraham Lincoln have far overrun their deployments, forces have rotated from Venezuela/Caribbean operations to the Middle East, and maintenance and training cycles are slipping.
insights.speaker: Ari Tabatabai
insights.so_what: Deferred maintenance and fleet overuse imply a large repair and recapitalization bill after the war, a tailwind for shipyards and defense maintenance.

insights.claim: Moving US military assets into the Middle East for the Iran war is leaving significant gaps in the Indo-Pacific, which serving general and flag officers have acknowledged on the record.
insights.speaker: Ari Tabatabai
insights.so_what: Weaker US deterrence in Asia raises Taiwan and South China Sea tail risk while US forces are tied down in the Gulf.
insights.quote: potentially leaving significant gaps in the Indoacific

insights.claim: The panel says the war has so far only set back some Iranian missile and drone sites, not achieved a strategic result, while costing billions of dollars in damaged US installations and thousands of lives across the region.
insights.speaker: Ari Tabatabai
insights.so_what: With costs rising and gains marginal, political pressure to settle is building, but on Iran's terms.

insights.claim: The administration cut the National Security Council from about 160 career detailees to below Eisenhower-era levels (at one point a public figure of 36 staff) and required Stephen Miller's personal permission before assistant-secretary and deputies-level interagency meetings could be held.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: Crisis contingencies are barely being planned for, so expect more unforeseen second-order shocks (evacuations, energy, alliances) in any US-led conflict.
insights.quote: less than 50 uh at one point 36 uh was the public number

insights.claim: The breakdown in interagency planning meant the US did not plan for a Hormuz closure, for the Supreme Leader's replacement after he was killed, for regional bases becoming unusable, for the global economic hit, or even for evacuating about half a million Americans from the region.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: Risks that were foreseeable are being priced late, because US policy responds after the fact and doesn't anticipate them.

insights.claim: Buyouts, DOGE and targeted reductions in force pushed out national-security officers 20 to 25 years into their careers, which is the post-9/11 generation with Middle East war experience, right before the Iran conflict.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: The loss of expertise will last for years, so expect lower-quality US crisis execution beyond this war.
insights.quote: targeted people in about the 20 to 25 year marks of their career

insights.claim: Firing Joint Chiefs Chairman CQ Brown, the Chief of Naval Operations, and the Defense Intelligence Agency head (the latter over battle-damage assessments showing Iran still had a nuclear program) discouraged officials from giving the president unwelcome assessments before and during the Iran war.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: Upward information flow is distorted, so official US claims of military progress deserve a heavier discount.

insights.claim: The Pentagon's civilian policy office, which normally weighs trade-offs, off-ramps and force allocation between combatant commanders, was sidelined in planning the Iran war.
insights.speaker: Ari Tabatabai
entities: Office of the Secretary of Defense
insights.so_what: Force allocation and exit planning are poor, which makes a longer, costlier war more likely.

insights.claim: The panel argues the Iran war was lost in Washington through the dismantling of process and expertise long before it was lost militarily in the Strait of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Julia Curley
insights.so_what: The analysts expect US strategic setbacks to continue as long as governance capacity is not rebuilt.
insights.quote: The the losing of this war it was lost in Washington long before it was lost in the straight of Hormuz.
